questions.q: In Mark 1:35, when did Jesus withdraw to a desolate place to pray?
options: At midday, once the crowds had been fed
Only after the disciples reminded him
On the Sabbath, instead of teaching
Very early in the morning, while it was still dark, after an overwhelmingly demanding day
questions.explanation: After a day of teaching, healing and meeting 'the whole city' at the door, he got up before anyone else could reach him.

questions.q: According to Matthew 14:13, what did Jesus do after hearing that John the Baptist had been killed?
options: He withdrew by boat to a solitary place
He immediately confronted Herod
He called the twelve together for a meal
He preached a sermon about John
questions.explanation: The timing invites us to see withdrawal as an appropriate response in a season of loss. Seeking solitude after loss is not weakness.

questions.q: What did Jesus do the night before choosing the twelve apostles (Luke 6:12–13)?
options: He fasted for forty days
He spent the whole night in prayer to God, then made the choice when day came
He asked the crowd to vote
He consulted the Pharisees
questions.explanation: Direction came after the withdrawal, not instead of it. The lesson is not that every decision needs a sleepless night, but that Jesus gave serious, undistracted attention to prayer before a significant choice.

questions.q: What does the chapter say was the consistent centre of Jesus' withdrawals?
options: Physical rest and recovery
Silence and reflection for their own sake
Prayer, communion with the Father
Escaping the demands of the crowd
questions.explanation: Silence, reflection and rest may accompany a Christian retreat, but they are not its centre. We do not withdraw merely to become calmer; we withdraw to become present to God.

questions.q: What does the chapter conclude from the times Jesus' solitude was interrupted (Mark 1:36–37; Matthew 14:13–23)?
options: An interruption automatically ruins a retreat and it must be restarted
Jesus never allowed interruptions
Interruptions are a sign that God does not want you to retreat
Respond to genuine needs, return to the quiet when possible, and reschedule what you cannot complete; the time given to God was not wasted
questions.explanation: After the crowds found him and he fed the five thousand, Matthew 14:23 says he went up the mountain alone to pray. He got his time alone; it just came later.

questions.q: Why does the chapter mention that Jesus took Peter, James and John to the Transfiguration and to Gethsemane?
options: To show that his example leaves room for both private solitude and supported retreat; isolation from people is not the goal
To show that solitude is unnecessary
To show that friends will always let you down
To recommend that retreats always be taken in groups of three
questions.explanation: They were imperfect companions, yet Jesus still allowed them near. This is why even the personal version of this retreat asks you to tell at least one person what you are doing.

reflection: Of the five moments listed above, which one is closest to where you are right now: after demand, in loss, before a decision, in a season of testing, or facing something hard? Write a sentence about why.
Jesus told the Father exactly what he wanted in Gethsemane. When did you last pray a prayer that honest? What stops you?
Who is one trustworthy person you could tell about this retreat? If no one comes to mind, what pastor, counsellor, mature believer, or supportive community could you begin approaching?
What would help you reduce avoidable interruptions without becoming anxious or resentful when a genuine need arises?
